blocks.title: Position and regions
blocks.md: Cameroon lies in Central and West Africa, at the head of the Gulf of Guinea, and is often called ‘Africa in miniature’ because it contains coast, forest, mountain, savanna and semi-desert. Neighbours: Nigeria, Chad, the Central African Republic, the Republic of the Congo, Gabon and Equatorial Guinea. It has **10 regions**: Adamawa, Centre, East, Far North, Littoral, North, North-West, South, South-West and West.

blocks.title: Relief
blocks.md: **Coastal plain** (Atlantic coast, mangroves, the Wouri estuary); **southern plateau** covered by equatorial forest; **western highlands** with volcanic mountains, including **Mount Cameroon** (over 4000 m, the highest peak in West and Central Africa); **Adamawa plateau** in the centre; **northern plains** of the Benue valley and the Lake Chad basin. Main rivers include the Sanaga, Wouri, Nyong and Benue.

items.text: North: Benue and Lake Chad plains (savanna, Sahel)

blocks.caption: A south-north sequence of physical regions (schematic, south at the bottom).
blocks.alt: Four stacked boxes: Atlantic coast, southern plateau, Adamawa plateau and northern plains, from bottom to top.

blocks.title: Climate and land use
blocks.md: The south has hot, humid equatorial climate and forest, with cocoa, plantain and timber. The coast and western highlands are very wet, with plantations and, in the highlands, coffee and food crops. The Adamawa plateau is cooler savanna suited to cattle. The north is hotter and drier, with cotton, millet, sorghum and pastoralism.

blocks.title: Be accurate
blocks.md:
- The country’s capital is Yaoundé (Centre); Douala (Littoral) is the largest city and main port.
- Mount Cameroon is in the South-West region; Lake Chad borders the Far North.
- Do not give precise areas or populations unless certain.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Region and activity
blocks.statement: Match a farming system to the physical conditions of the western highlands.
steps: Volcanic soils and cooler temperatures at altitude.
Good rainfall and relief rain on slopes.
Coffee, maize, vegetables and dense rural population.
blocks.answer: Coffee and mixed food farming on fertile volcanic soils.

blocks.title: Example 2 — North-south contrast
blocks.statement: Describe the change in climate from south to north and its effects on vegetation.
steps: Rainfall decreases and the dry season lengthens northwards.
Equatorial forest gives way to savanna, then to Sahelian thorn scrub.
Farming shifts from cocoa and plantain to cotton, millet and herding.
blocks.answer: A drier, more seasonal climate and open savanna in the north.

blocks.title: Physical features
blocks.md: Africa straddles the equator, so climate zones are arranged in a roughly symmetrical pattern: equatorial rainforest (Congo Basin and Gulf of Guinea), tropical savanna to the north and south, then the Sahel and Sahara in the north and the Kalahari and Namib in the south, with Mediterranean climates at the northern and southern tips. Features: the **Sahara**, the **Congo Basin**, the **Great Rift Valley** and its lakes, the Ethiopian Highlands, the Atlas and Drakensberg mountains.

blocks.title: Rivers and resources
blocks.md: Major rivers: the **Nile** (flowing north to the Mediterranean), **Niger**, **Congo** and **Zambezi**. Resources include oil and gas in several countries, minerals such as copper and diamonds in central and southern Africa, cocoa and coffee in West and East Africa, and hydropower potential on the large rivers. Many countries remain dependent on exporting raw materials.

blocks.caption: Africa’s five regions and a few typical features.
blocks.alt: A two-column table listing each African sub-region and typical physical features.

blocks.title: Regional groupings
blocks.md: Africa is commonly divided into **North, West, Central, East and Southern** Africa. The **African Union (AU)** brings together the continent’s states; regional economic communities, such as ECOWAS (West), CEMAC (Central) and EAC (East), promote trade and cooperation. Development patterns differ widely, so avoid describing the continent as uniform.

blocks.title: Avoid these errors
blocks.md:
- Africa is a continent of many countries, climates and cultures; do not treat it as one place.
- The Nile flows northwards.
- The Sahel is not the Sahara: it is the semi-arid transition belt to the south.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Why are climate zones symmetrical?
blocks.statement: Explain why similar climates appear north and south of the equator in Africa.
steps: The equator lies near the middle of the continent.
Pressure belts and the ITCZ are arranged symmetrically around the equator.
Rainfall decreases with distance from the equatorial belt on both sides.
blocks.answer: Symmetry of the global circulation around the equator.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Resource dependence
blocks.statement: Explain why countries that rely on one exported resource may face economic problems.
steps: Little processing means little added value and fewer jobs.
Diversification into manufacturing and services reduces risk.
blocks.answer: Price instability and low added value.

blocks.title: Enquiry process
blocks.md: 1. Question or hypothesis. 2. Methods: questionnaires, measurements, counts, interviews, secondary data. 3. **Sampling** (random, systematic, stratified). 4. Risk assessment and ethics. 5. Presentation (graphs, maps, tables). 6. Analysis with statistics. 7. Conclusion and evaluation of reliability and bias.

blocks.title: Spearman’s rank
blocks.md: Rank both variables, find the difference d between ranks for each pair, then $r_s = 1 - \frac{6 \sum d^2}{n(n^2 - 1)}$. A value near +1 shows strong positive correlation, near −1 strong negative, near 0 none. Compare with a critical value to test significance (given in tables).

blocks.caption: The stages of a geographical enquiry.
blocks.alt: Four boxes: question, methods and sampling, collect and present, analyse conclude evaluate.

blocks.title: Interpreting results
blocks.md: A strong correlation does not prove one variable causes the other. Small samples may be unreliable, and a fieldwork site may not represent the whole area. Always comment on the limits and suggest improvements.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Calculate
blocks.statement: Five towns are ranked by size (x) and by number of services (y). Ranks of the pairs (x, y) are (1,2), (2,1), (3,4), (4,3), (5,5). Calculate Spearman’s r_s.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Choose sampling
blocks.statement: A student surveys a 400-house district divided into four equal neighbourhoods. She needs 40 houses. Name an unbiased method.
steps: Stratified: sample proportionally from each neighbourhood.
10 houses per neighbourhood, chosen at random from each list.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Describe the causes and effects of desertification in the Sahel and suggest two management strategies.
exercises.model: Causes: drought, overgrazing, over-cultivation, fuelwood cutting, population pressure. Effects: soil erosion, lower yields, loss of pasture, food shortages and migration. Strategies: tree planting and shelterbelts (including the Great Green Wall); zaï pits and stone lines; improved stoves; rotational grazing. Local participation is key.
exercises.rubric: Causes (1); effects (1); two strategies with explanation (1); coherent answer (0).
exercises.explanation: Causes: drought, overgrazing, over-cultivation, fuelwood cutting, population pressure. Effects: soil erosion, lower yields, loss of pasture, food shortages and migration. Strategies: tree planting and shelterbelts (including the Great Green Wall); zaï pits and stone lines; improved stoves; rotational grazing. Local participation is key.
